title: Latin America's Fading Demographic Tailwind
gist: Latin America's decades-long demographic dividend from a rising working-age share — which helped more than double regional income per capita since 1960 — is peaking or already declining in Brazil, Chile, Colombia, and Costa Rica, while a contested new 'scarcity dividend' literature and generative AI are floated as the next possible growth engines if the region invests deliberately rather than just consumes the gains.

insights.claim: Since 1960, a rising working-age population share and shrinking share of children have been a distinct driver of growth in Latin America and the Caribbean, helping income per capita more than double from $3,336 to just over $9,000 as of last year.
insights.speaker: EDUARDO LEVY YEYATI AND RAFAEL ROFMAN
insights.so_what: Frames age structure as an underappreciated growth driver alongside the usual productivity/investment/institutions narrative, meaning growth forecasts that ignore demographics have been missing a real, now-fading, tailwind.
insights.quote: which more than doubled from $3,336 to just over $9,000 last year

insights.claim: The 'first dividend' framework holds that, all else equal, GDP per capita rises roughly one-for-one with the working-age population share: a 10% increase in the working-age share translates into about a 10% increase in GDP per capita if labor force participation and productivity stay constant.
insights.speaker: EDUARDO LEVY YEYATI AND RAFAEL ROFMAN
insights.so_what: Gives investors a simple mental model to back out how much of a country's past GDP-per-capita growth was demographic mechanics versus genuine productivity gains — and thus how much is durable.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "All things being equal, a larger working-age population"

insights.claim: Economists Rainer Kotschy and David E. Bloom, using a panel of 145 countries from 1950 to 2015, found in 2023 that a 1% rise in the working-age population share raises income per capita by roughly 0.8% to 1%, supporting a near one-for-one demographic effect.
insights.speaker: EDUARDO LEVY YEYATI AND RAFAEL ROFMAN
insights.so_what: This is the empirical anchor for sizing the growth impact as the working-age share now falls in several Latin American economies — a directly usable coefficient for back-of-envelope growth modeling.
insights.quote: a 1% rise in the working-age share raises income per capita by roughly 0.8% to 1%
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "All things being equal, a larger working-age population"

insights.claim: The size and timing of the demographic bonus varies sharply across Latin America: the working-age population increase ranges from 11% in Uruguay to more than 45% in Colombia, the Dominican Republic, and Honduras, and the 'positive slope' period lasts roughly 40 years in some countries versus nearly 80 in others.
insights.speaker: EDUARDO LEVY YEYATI AND RAFAEL ROFMAN
insights.so_what: Country selection within Latin America should account for how much demographic tailwind is left, not treat the region as a bloc — Uruguay's smaller, shorter bonus contrasts sharply with Colombia's larger one.
insights.quote: from an 11% increase in the working-age population in Uruguay to more than 45% in Colombia, the Dominican Republic, and Honduras
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Applied to Latin America since 2000"

themes.theme: Where each country sits on the curve

insights.claim: Brazil, Chile, Colombia, and Costa Rica have already passed the peak of their demographic tailwind and will see it gradually decline from here.
insights.speaker: EDUARDO LEVY YEYATI AND RAFAEL ROFMAN
insights.so_what: These four economies face a structural, multi-decade demographic headwind to per-capita growth going forward, independent of cyclical or policy factors — a factor to build into long-horizon growth and equity-market return assumptions for these markets.
insights.quote: Brazil, Chile, Colombia, and Costa Rica’s tailwinds have already peaked and will gradually decline.

insights.claim: Argentina, Ecuador, Mexico, Panama, Peru, and Uruguay still have roughly a decade of growing first-dividend tailwind remaining, while countries further behind in the demographic transition have even longer runways.
insights.speaker: EDUARDO LEVY YEYATI AND RAFAEL ROFMAN
insights.so_what: This group retains a roughly 10-year demographic growth cushion relative to Brazil/Chile/Colombia/Costa Rica, a relevant differentiator for relative-value country allocation within Latin America.
insights.quote: Others—including Argentina, Ecuador, Mexico, Panama, Peru, and Uruguay—still have about a decade of a growing first dividend

insights.claim: Japan illustrates the far side of the demographic cycle: from 2000 to last year, demography subtracted about 0.57 percentage points per year from Japan's headline growth, meaning its GDP per working-age person grew faster than aggregate GDP per capita implies; China has already passed its peak working-age share and South Korea is quickly moving into the same drag.
insights.speaker: EDUARDO LEVY YEYATI AND RAFAEL ROFMAN
insights.so_what: Japan's ~0.57pp/year demographic drag is a concrete, quantified preview of the multi-decade headwind now beginning for Brazil, Chile, Colombia, and Costa Rica, useful for sizing the eventual downside to their trend growth.
insights.quote: demography subtracted about 0.57 percentage points per year from growth

themes.theme: The second dividend is a political choice, not automatic

insights.claim: A durable 'second dividend' only materializes if part of the income gains from the first (demographic) dividend are reinvested to raise productivity, rather than consumed — a serious political challenge in a region marked by high poverty and inequality, where the pull toward higher consumption now competes with the need for higher saving and investment for the future.
insights.speaker: EDUARDO LEVY YEYATI AND RAFAEL ROFMAN
insights.so_what: Whether a country locks in durable growth after its demographic window closes depends on a specific, trackable policy choice (savings/investment rate vs. consumption), not on demographics alone — a useful screen for judging which Latin American governments are actually banking their dividend.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "That calls attention to the second dividend"

insights.claim: The authors argue Latin America's demographic tailwind was probably larger than conservative accounting captures, which means its eventual exhaustion will be a bigger downward adjustment to absorb than typically assumed, not a smaller one.
insights.speaker: EDUARDO LEVY YEYATI AND RAFAEL ROFMAN
insights.so_what: Warns against complacency: consensus growth models may be underestimating how much of Latin America's past growth was demographic borrowing, implying a larger-than-expected growth air-pocket as the tailwind fades.
insights.quote: which makes its future exhaustion a bigger adjustment to absorb, not a smaller one
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "If anything, Latin America’s demographic tailwind"

insights.claim: A new paper by economists Daron Acemoglu, David Autor, Keelan Beirne, and Andrew Scott, using a global cross-country panel back to 1950 and data on 722 U.S. commuting zones, finds lower birth rates tied to faster growth in GDP per working-age adult with no clear loss in total output, as areas where young workers grew scarce saw more labor-saving patents and high-tech investment.
insights.speaker: EDUARDO LEVY YEYATI AND RAFAEL ROFMAN
insights.so_what: If this 'scarcity dividend' effect holds for Latin America, a fading demographic tailwind need not be a growth drag — it could instead spur automation investment, an important upside scenario for long-run Latin American productivity that runs against conventional aging-is-bad narratives.
insights.quote: lower birth rates were tied to faster growth in GDP per working-age adult, with no clear loss in total output

insights.claim: A separate study by Maestas, Mullen, and Powell on the U.S. found aging associated with slower productivity growth, directly at odds with the Acemoglu et al. 'scarcity dividend' finding; the authors reconcile this by arguing the scarcity-to-innovation channel is conditional on having the capital markets and R&D infrastructure needed to convert scarce labor into automation.
insights.speaker: EDUARDO LEVY YEYATI AND RAFAEL ROFMAN
insights.so_what: This is the crux for Latin America specifically: the 'scarcity dividend' only pays off where capital markets and R&D infrastructure exist to convert labor scarcity into automation investment — infrastructure much of the region currently lacks, making the upside scenario conditional rather than automatic.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Studying the U.S., Maestas, Mullen, and Powell"

themes.theme: The policy playbook and AI as the next engine

insights.claim: The authors' policy prescription to offset the fading first dividend and to build the capacity to capture a scarcity dividend is the same list: higher female labor-force participation, longer working lives, migration where politically feasible, and productivity investment across education, capital allocation, competition, infrastructure, and technology diffusion.
insights.speaker: EDUARDO LEVY YEYATI AND RAFAEL ROFMAN
insights.so_what: This is an explicit checklist for scoring which Latin American governments are actually positioning for a post-demographic-dividend economy versus which are not.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "The appropriate policy response follows"

insights.claim: Latin American countries have historically performed poorly on most of these productivity levers — citing poor learning outcomes, failing infrastructure, and low savings and investment as common regional weaknesses — which the authors say must be reversed to narrow the gap with more developed economies.
insights.speaker: EDUARDO LEVY YEYATI AND RAFAEL ROFMAN
insights.so_what: A blunt admission from the authors that the region's institutional starting point is weak on exactly the levers needed to replace the fading demographic tailwind, tempering optimism about an automatic 'second dividend.'
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "The appropriate policy response follows"

insights.claim: The authors frame generative AI as 'the live test' of whether Latin America can convert investment into productivity gains — a new potential growth engine arriving just as the demographic one fades, but one that, unlike the automatic demographic dividend, must be deliberately built and could cause more disruption than the demographic transition if mismanaged.
insights.speaker: EDUARDO LEVY YEYATI AND RAFAEL ROFMAN
insights.so_what: Positions AI adoption policy in Latin America as the single most consequential near-term lever for whether the region avoids a Japan-style demographic growth air-pocket — a thesis worth tracking via regional AI investment and digital-infrastructure data.
insights.quote: Generative AI is the live test of that bet.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "The tailwind generated by the demographic bonus"

source_meta.author: EDUARDO LEVY YEYATI AND RAFAEL ROFMAN
